newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: U.S. seeks three new members to NATO.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks three new members to NATO.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright goes into NATO talks on Thursday representing a U.S. position in favour of inviting three rather than five or more former Warsaw Pact states as new members of the Western alliance, U.S. officials say.

Although some officials do not rule out political manoeuvring that could alter that view, the Clinton administration consensus favours extending membership this year to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic while holding a decision on other potential candidates -- such as Romania and Slovenia -- for a later date.
That is the safest serious option under discussion in what is arguably the most far-reaching and controversial U.S. foreign policy initiative of the post-Cold War era.
Albright, who earlier attended a U.S.-European Union summit in The Hague, flew to Portugal on Wednesday night.

She will attend a NATO foreign ministers meeting on Thursday at a luxury resort outside Lisbon that is to begin laying the groundwork for deciding which countries will be invited to join the alliance when its 16 leaders meet in Madrid on July 8-9.

Unlike many other countries, the United States has not publicly announced its preferred candidates for NATO expansion. But in interviews, officials throughout the government have said that the consensus favours membership this year for Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic only despite strong campaigns by Romania and Slovenia.

White House press secretary Mike McCurry indirectly affirmed this view at a news conference earlier this week in Paris. Asked if the U.S. view still reflected a preference for Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic as reported in the media, he said: "Our thinking is very much along the lines you've seen reported."

Extending the NATO security umbrella to former Cold War enemies is already fanning intense debate in the United States and the subject is expected to become more contentious. The U.S. Senate, as well as parliaments in other NATO member states, must approve enlargement.

France is championing Romania's cause while Italy is pushing Slovenia. Many experts say if the United States, as NATO's leading member, could be persuaded to their cause, Romania and Slovenia would also gain membership this year.

For various reasons, U.S. officials believe that despite strides, the two countries need to continue working on democratic economic, political and military reforms before being accepted for membership.
Also, they argue that passing over Romania and Slovenia this time ensures there will be a second round of NATO enlargement sometime in the near future.

U.S. officials do not expect the NATO foreign ministers to settle the question of new members at Thursday's meeting. There are other opportunities for discussion, such as the summit of major industrialised powers plus Russia in Denver, Colorado next month.
Albright is also expected to push her NATO counterparts to commit themselves to revive efforts to ensure that the 1995 U.S.-brokered Dayton peace accords that ended the Bosnia war is a success.
This includes ensuring the safe return of refugees, the apprehension and trial of war criminals and the building of institutions that support a unified, multi-ethnic state in Bosnia.
Albright is due to visit Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia at the weekend to press the leaders there to implement the peace deal.
